We derive 7 explicit regularity of the original action marginal in a constrained invest- 7 8 ment economy with continuous innovations and nested average value at 8 9 risk, including binding capacities and moving adverse tails. Complete proofs preserve the own-future 13 14 construction and qualified links to stochastic control and nonlinear re- 14 15 cursive utility. An independent comparison fixes 56 learned actors across 15 16 two risk levels, two information budgets, seven representations and two 16 learning losses, alongside an original-model online control. INTRODUCTION 1 2 1 2 3 A dynamic decision maker buys an approximation because it changes the cost 3 4 of making a good decision. In a constrained investment problem, an accurate 4 5 continuation level can still give the wrong incentive to invest, while a continuation 5 6 with a large common level error can choose the correct action. Under recursive 6 7 risk, the difficulty is greater: changing a continuation can also change which shocks 7 8 receive adverse weight. A numerical method must therefore connect its acquired 8 9 information, its fitted critic, its feasible actor and its computational work to the 9 10 original recursive objective. 10 11 Neural Bellman Operators (NBOs) address this chain by constructing and learn- 11 12 ing recursive continuation operators together with an account of their policy error. 12 13 The object is the Bellman operator of the specified economy. Its criterion, infor- 13 14 mation filtration, constraints and boundary conditions remain part of that object 14 15 throughout approximation and deployment. The paper retains both a constructive 15 16 own-future neural operator and an analysis of arbitrary acquired critics. It develops 16 17 their links with stochastic control and, under separate explicit assumptions, nonlin- 17 18 ear Brownian recursive utility. A result for the nested risk investment application is 18 19 not automatically a welfare improvement in a different expected-utility or nonlinear 19 20 recursive-utility model. 20 21 The central computational question is which continuation information is worth 22 acquiring. Earlier NBO calculations found a concrete mismatch: every certificate- 22 23 oriented fit in a retained comparison reduced a residual-span criterion, but the aggre- 23 24 gate number of rejected first actions increased from 644 to 757. The quadratic control 24 25 remained a strong complete-service baseline. The subsequent policy-comparison 25 26 calculations preserved that economic criterion and constructed safe actual improve- 26 27 ments, yet acquisition still used a value loss. Those results motivate a new learning 27 28 calculation in the original model. Their observations and costs retain their historical 28 29 identities in the development companion; the present sample does not reuse them. 29 30 We learn the marginal continuation cost after evaluating the original risk operator. 30 21 31 This order matters. In the two-date investment economy, the original optimal 31 32 continuation is the last-date Bellman image of the known terminal function. It is 32 NEURAL BELLMAN OPERATORS 3 1 acquired through paid outward calculations. The root critic retains the known action 2 cost and learns the action-dependent part of the integrated continuation. A state- 2 3 only anchor completes its value level. The resulting actor is proposed by piecewise 3 4 minimization of that learned objective over the original capacity interval. Floating 4 5 critical-point calculations generate a proposal; admission requires a certificate for 5 6 the original complete policy. The same acquired values, features where relevant, 6 7 feasible actions and certification rules are available to the conventional controls. 7 8 1 The mathematical contribution has three connected parts. First, we derive a con- 8 9 tinuous original-action marginal and explicit moduli from the nonlinear investment 9 10 technology, binding capacity and moving AVaR tails. The central interval excluded 10 11 from the adverse tail can touch either shock boundary. Its variational inequalities 11 12 control movement of the tail without differentiating a numerical sort or an un- 12 13 constrained optimizer. Finite original-risk value enclosures then provide outward 13 14 derivative labels, with the precision cost of finite differences paid explicitly. 14 15 Second, a bounded readout is fitted to minimize the worst action-marginal dis- 15 16 crepancy over those outward labels. The finite training problem is convex for each 16 17 declared feature family. Exact primal and dual bounds certify the actual stored 17 18 coefficients without treating a floating solver’s success flag as a proof. An explicit 18 19 feature-range construction states how to extend the acquired information to off- 19 20 design action comparisons. Its integral along the feasible action path controls policy 20 21 loss and possible policy changes; a capacity-sensitive stationarity bound sharpens 21 22 the account when available. The argument applies to a nonconvex fitted polyno- 22 23 mial or spline through the all-action comparison, and never assumes that target 23 24 smoothness removes a fitted ReLU kink. This extension is a proved construction 24 25 whose numerical cell bounds and cost must also be supplied before it can certify an 25 26 off-design decision. The current experiment audits the finite-node fits and admits 26 27 policies through the separate original-model certificate; it does not claim to have 27 28 executed that global feature-cell calculation. 28 29 Third, we state what is lost if the critic’s anchor is discarded recursively. In 29 30 this very investment transition, a state-dependent continuation level that does not 30 31 change a last-date action can shift the root marginal by a known nonzero amount. 31 32 A full level-and-contrast recursion therefore carries the anchor error, the action gap 32 4 1 and the future policy error separately. A noncash-invariant recursive preference 1 2 receives its own continuation Lipschitz account. It cannot inherit a monetary shift 2 3 identity merely because both criteria have a Bellman notation. 3 4 Derivative-assisted economic dynamic programming already uses Hermite ap- 4 5 proximation with value and slope information (Cai and Judd, 2015). Derivative 6 supervision and task-based model learning also have established precedents (Czar- 6 7 necki et al., 2017, Donti et al., 2017, Elmachtoub and Grigas, 2022). The training 7 8 certificates use convex duality and affine supporting bounds; these general tools do 8 9 not themselves supply a claim of methodological novelty. The development history 9 10 also contains certificate-aware readouts and an action-null quotient analysis. The 10 11 additional results here concern their explicit construction and verification for the 11 12 original recursive risk operator, including tail changes, paid finite-risk information, 12 13 feasible actions and recursive value levels. A three-probe lower bound identifies 13 14 a limitation of that stated information interface; it is not a lower bound for every 14 15 algorithm with access to the investment formulas. 15 5 16 The numerical comparison changes the learning loss before changing the evalua- 16 17 tion sample. Two separately executed acquisition budgets use nested state designs. 17 18 Seven stored representations each have a value-loss and an action-marginal-loss 18 19 critic; the online original-model method is included at both risk levels. Quadratic, 19 20 polynomial, cubic spline, multilinear grid and semi-analytic controls form the 20 21 conventional menu. An exactly corresponding hinge encoding makes the neural 21 22 representation claim testable: a geometry shared with that control is not a uniquely 22 23 neural contribution. 23 24 The protocol fixes 64 new independent initial states, complete original-policy 24 25 evaluation, five fresh matched timing processes, exact independent reconstruction, 25 26 simultaneous positive and adverse gain inference and full acquisition/service cost 26 27 comparisons. It also fixes how unresolved and failed calculations are retained. ECONOMIC USE AND THE REMAINING RESEARCH TASK 24 25 The role of a Neural Bellman Operator is to acquire and reuse continuation 26 information that changes feasible economic decisions at an acceptable total cost. 26 27 The new construction supplies original-marginal regularity, paid derivative labels, 27 28 checked finite-box fitting gaps and sufficient action conditions under the original 28 29 recursive risk objective. The implemented MARGINAL learner nevertheless raises 29 30 the independently enclosed sample mean cost in every loss comparison, and its 30 31 timing improvements are a minority of the complete records. This campaign has 31 32 not established the intended neural economic or computational advantage. The re- 32 25 NEURAL BELLMAN OPERATORS 35 1 search objective remains a competitive learned recursive Bellman operator, with the 2 original model, strong controls and full decision costs determining that comparison. 2 3 The action bounds specify a concrete route for further algorithmic work. An 3 4 original derivative enclosure can stop regret certification when its capacity-sensitive 4 5 bound plus the future-policy allowance meets the economic tolerance. A proposed 5 6 policy change requires the original continuation contrast bound, including that 6 7 allowance, to certify improvement. Building these bounds from the learned critic 7 8 requires the feature-range and off-design calculations in Theorem 9; the current 8 9 finite-node fitting audit does not provide them. The simultaneous event results 9 10 preserve both potential gains and harms across states, but they do not implement a 10 11 selection rule. Using independent evaluation labels to choose the favorable actions 11 12 afterwards would give the selector information and cost treatment absent from the 12 13 frozen experiment. 13 14 1 Precision allocation must therefore be tied to a decision that the additional in- 14 15 formation can resolve. Taking closer finite-difference probes while leaving the 15 16 value enclosures unchanged can amplify uncertainty through division by the probe 16 17 distance. Increasing the state grid also costs more without guaranteeing a better 17 18 feasible action, as the complete budget comparison shows. The proved path and 18 19 stationarity conditions identify valid stopping tests; the cost of acquiring them, 19 20 the choice of refinement and a safe deployable selector remain to be demonstrated 20 21 under a new independent protocol. The existing probe radius, grids, models and 21 22 evaluation states are unchanged by this interpretation. They do not establish scalability 26 in horizon, state dimension or innovation dimension. The retained theorems de- 26 27 scribe those separate objects and their assumptions; their historical experiments 27 28 and unresolved regions remain in the development companion.
